turns.content: I am comparing the ages of five isolated, solar-metallicity stars under the same assumptions about rotation, mixing, and initial conditions: a 5-solar-mass RGB star; a 1-solar-mass star at 5700 K with log g = 4.2; a 1-solar-mass RGB star; a 1-solar-mass star at 5760 K with log g = 4.45; and a 1-solar-mass AGB star. Which physical properties should guide the age comparison?
How does initial mass set the evolutionary timescale, and why can a 5-solar-mass giant be younger than a less-evolved 1-solar-mass star?
What does that mass-dependent lifetime comparison imply for the age of the 5-solar-mass RGB star relative to all four 1-solar-mass stars?
Now compare the two 1-solar-mass stars specified by temperature and surface gravity. Which is less evolved, and what does the difference in log g imply about their relative ages?
Where should the 1-solar-mass RGB and AGB stars fall relative to those two 1-solar-mass main-sequence or near-subgiant stars? Please use the standard evolutionary sequence.
Can you assemble those comparisons into a complete youngest-to-oldest sequence, identifying each star by its physical properties rather than by a letter?
How certain is that ordering given that we do not have full stellar-evolution tracks or uncertainties for the measured temperatures and surface gravities?
Please cross-check the sequence against both mass-dependent stellar lifetimes and the main-sequence-to-RGB-to-AGB progression at one solar mass.
Give the final increasing-age sequence and the main physical reason for each adjacent comparison.
